p.x:
In my school, we have a small robot called Bobo. Bobo can talk and answer simple questions. It has a funny voice and big blue eyes. When you say "Hello," it says, "Hello, human!"
Our teacher says Bobo is a tool to help us learn. It can't think like a person because it doesn't have a real brain. But it can tell us the weather, play music and help us practise English words.
I think robots will be very important in the future. Maybe one day every home will have a robot to cook and clean. I want to learn how to build robots when I grow up!

You may not notice it, but you probably use artificial intelligence every day. When your phone unlocks with facial recognition, that's AI. When a music app recommends songs you might like, that's AI too. Many people use a voice assistant to set alarms or check the weather, or ask a chatbot for help with homework.
AI works through machine learning. Instead of following a fixed program, the software learns patterns from large amounts of data. The more data it sees, the better its accuracy becomes. However, AI can still make errors, so it's important to check its answers.
AI is also used with robots. In factories, automation means that machines do repetitive work. Some companies are even building humanoid robots that look and move like people. Engineers use computers to simulate how robots will move before they build the expensive hardware.
Not everyone is happy about these changes. Some people worry about job loss and unemployment if robots replace human workers. Others raise questions of ethics: is it OK for students to copy answers from AI? Is a virtual friend as good as a real one? Experts agree that AI can be intelligent in some ways, but it is very different from a human.

The idea of thinking machines has fascinated humans for centuries, from ancient myths to the androids of science fiction. Today, with the rapid development of large AI models, the question has become urgent rather than theoretical.
Modern AI systems are built on neural networks, mathematical structures loosely inspired by the human brain. Trained on enormous amounts of training data, they can write essays, create images and answer complex questions in response to a simple prompt. Their abilities can appear almost magical, yet they have significant weaknesses. Chatbots sometimes hallucinate, confidently presenting false information as fact, and they may reproduce biases found in their data. Meanwhile, deepfakes, realistic but fake videos and audio, threaten to undermine trust in what we see and hear.
These developments raise difficult questions of accountability. If an AI system gives harmful medical advice or makes an unfair decision about a loan, who is responsible: the developer, the company that uses it, or the user? Governments around the world are now drafting laws to address such issues.
The economic impact is equally debated. Optimists argue that AI will augment human workers rather than replace them, handling routine tasks while people focus on creative and social work. Pessimists warn that millions will need to reskill, and not everyone will manage. Beyond these practical concerns lie deeper philosophical questions. Could a machine ever possess consciousness? And if superintelligence, an AI far more capable than any human, were ever developed, could we ensure it shared our values? There are no easy answers, but the debate is no longer only for science-fiction writers.
